parole.significato: An irrigation ditch, chiefly with reference to Mexico or the southwestern US.
parole.testo: From Spanish acequia, from Arabic الساقیة (“water conduit”), ultimately from Classical Arabic سَقَى (saqā, “to irrigate”). Doublet of sakia.

parole.significato: The governor or commander of a Spanish or Portuguese fortress or prison.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish alcaide, from Arabic الْقَائِد (al-qāʔid, “leader”); Doublet of caid and Alkaid.

parole.significato: In Spain or Latin America, a municipal magistrate who has both judicial and administrative functions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish alcalde, from Arabic اَلْقَاضِي (al-qāḍī, “the judge”). Doublet of qadi and casis.

parole.significato: A Bush, henna (Lawsonia inermis).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish alcana, alheña, from Arabic الحِنَّاء (al-ḥinnāʔ, “henna”). Compare also alkanet.

parole.significato: a jug, pitcher, etc. made of porous earthenware.
parole.testo: From Spanish alcarraza, from Arabic الكُرَّاز (al-kurrāz), from Aramaic כרז / כרוז (“a type of container”), possibly from Akkadian 𒆳𒍣𒍝𒆪 (/⁠kurziza, kurzizakku⁠/, “a basket, container”), from Sumerian 𒄥𒋛𒁲 (/⁠gursisa⁠/, “basket, container”, literally “normal or standard 𒄥 (gur)”).

parole.significato: Any Moorish fortress in Spain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish alcázar, from Arabic الْقَصْر (al-qaṣr). Doublet of castle.

parole.significato: A plant, principally of Medicago sativa, grown as a pasture crop.

parole.significato: An Islamic cleric, an expert in Islamic law and jurisprudence, especially in medieval and early modern Spain.
parole.testo: From Spanish alfaquí, from Arabic الفَقِيه (al-faqīh, “the theologian”), from فَقِهَ (faqiha, “to be wise”).

parole.significato: A solitaire card game played with two decks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish Alhambra, from Arabic الْحَمْرَاء (al-ḥamrāʔ, “the red (fortress)”).

parole.significato: Text of non-Semitic languages, especially European languages, written in Arabic letters.
parole.testo: From Spanish aljamiado (composed of aljamía + -ado), from Arabic عَجَمِيَّة (ʕajamiyya) or اَلْعَجَمِيَّة (al-ʕajamiyya), from عَجَم (ʕajam, “non-Arabs, esp. Persians”) + ـِي (-ī, “relative adjective (nisba) suffix”) + ـَة (-a, “feminine marker, also used to mark language names or to generally form

parole.significato: Ruddle (red ochre), found in Spain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish almagra (more commonly almagre), from Arabic الْمُغْرَة (al-muḡra, “red clay or earth”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the doctrine and movement founded in 12th-century Morocco by Ibn Tumart.
parole.testo: From Spanish almohade, from Arabic مُوَحِّد (muwaḥḥid). Doublet of Muwahhid.

parole.significato: A member of a Berber dynasty that started in 11th-century Morocco.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish almorávide, from Arabic مُرَابِط (murābiṭ).

parole.significato: An ancient strategy board game, an ancestor of checkers, thought to have originated in the Middle East.
parole.testo: From Spanish alquerque, from Arabic القرقات.

parole.significato: A kettledrum; a kind of tabor used by the Moors.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish atabal, from Arabic الطَّبْل (aṭ-ṭabl, “drum”), طَبَلَ (ṭabala, “to drum”). Compare tabor, tymbal, tabla, davul.

parole.significato: A municipality or subdivision of a municipality in Spanish America, and in Spain itself.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish barrio, from Arabic بَرِّيّ (barriyy, “wild”).

parole.significato: Any of various marine fish of the genus Sarda that are related to and resemble the tuna, but smaller.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish bonito (“bonito”).

parole.significato: An inn or hotel in a Spanish-speaking country.
parole.testo: From Spanish fonda, from Arabic فُنْدُق (funduq, “inn, hotel; manor”), from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon), from πᾰν- (păn-, “all, every”) + the combining form of δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to receive”) + -εῖον (-eîon, “-ium: forming building names”). Doublet of fonduk and fondaco.

parole.significato: Synonym of vizier.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish alguacil, and then from Arabic وَزِير (wazīr, “helper, aide, minister”, literally “one who bears (the burden of office)”). Doublet of vizier.

parole.significato: A stringed musical instrument, of European origin, usually with a fretted fingerboard and six strings, played with the…
parole.testo: From Spanish guitarra, from Arabic قِيثَارَة (qīṯāra), from Ancient Greek κῐθᾰ́ρᾱ (kĭthắrā). Doublet of cithara, cither, and zither, but not related to sitar.

parole.testo: Macarena (“dance”) + wing. Coined by the popular media, named after the popular 1990s dance that originated from the dancing in the video for the eponymous 1990s song by Los Del Rios. parole.significato: A former Spanish coin and unit of currency, originally issued in gold but later in silver and copper, discontinued in 1…
parole.testo: From Spanish maravedí, from Arabic مُرَابِطِين (murābiṭīn), an inflected plural of مُرَابِط (murābiṭ, “holy man”), the name of the Almoravid rulers of Muslim Spain during the 12th century. Compare marabout.

parole.significato: A type of wooden rattle from Latin America.
parole.testo: From Spanish matraca, from dialectal Arabic مَطْرَق (maṭraq). See Aramaic מטרקא (mṭrqʾ) for more.

parole.significato: A Mediterranean dish consisting of filleted salt-cured tuna.
parole.testo: From Spanish mojama, from Arabic مُشَمَّع (mušammaʕ, “of wax”).

parole.significato: An Iberian Christian living under Arab domination.
parole.testo: From Spanish mozárabe, from Arabic مُسْتَعْرِب (mustaʕrib).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Moors of al-Andalus who remained in Christian territory after the Reconquista but were not conv…
parole.testo: From Spanish mudéjar, from Arabic مُدَجَّن (mudajjan, “domesticated”), from the verb دَجَّنَ (dajjana, “to tame”), from دَجَنَ (dajana, “to become accustomed”).

parole.significato: A treadwheel with attached buckets, used to raise and deposit water.
parole.testo: From Spanish noria, from Arabic نَاعُورَة (nāʕūra), from Classical Syriac ܢܥܘܪܬܐ (nāʿōrtāʾ, “water wheel; growler”), from ܢܥܪ (nʿar, “to roar, growl, bray”).

parole.significato: An enormous mythical bird in Eastern legend.
parole.testo: From Spanish rocho, ruc, from Arabic رُخّ (ruḵḵ), from Classical Persian رُخ (rux).

parole.significato: A Muslim principality on the Iberian Peninsula during the 11th, 12th and 13th centuries.
parole.testo: From Spanish taifa, from Arabic طَائِفَة (ṭāʔifa, “sect, faction”).
